title: Photoreal output, correct animation as control
subtitle: Experiment 6 · how little pose is enough?
footer: Experiment 6 · 10 AMASS/BABEL clips · 5 conditioning densities · 50 videos

intro.question: Given a clean motion-capture clip as depth control and a sentence for appearance, how few conditioned frames still produce the right action?
bullets: **Earlier experiments used a motion model's output as the control.** It often did not perform the action in the prompt at all, so we could never separate *did the video model improve the motion* from *can it rescue a motion that was never right*.
**Here the control is clean motion capture** — ten AMASS/BABEL clips that genuinely perform the action they are labelled with.
**The animation is control only.** We render it as a depth video and feed that in. Appearance comes from the text prompt, so the output is a photorealistic person in a real place.
**Then we pull the motion back out** with pose recovery and re-render it on the same neutral body, so the motion that came back can be compared with the motion that went in.
**The one variable is how many frames carry a pose** — 22 of them down to 2. Everything else is held fixed.

walk.prompt: a man walking along a city sidewalk
walk.headline: The action survives to two frames. The input's **path** does not — from K = 5 it walks straight across frame and never makes the turn.

run.prompt: a man running on an outdoor running track
run.headline: Same threshold as walk, sharper. From K = 5 it is a generic run — and foot skate goes from 180 mm/s in to **900–1800 mm/s out**.

jump.headline: The error steps up at K = 8 and then never gets worse. The crouch-and-launch survives to two frames — and from K = 8 the model adds a **basketball** the control never contained.

kick.headline: **The only clip that loses its action.** At K = 3 and K = 2 the kick is gone; what is left is footwork with one late leg raise.

sit_down.prompt: a man lowering himself into a seated position
sit_down.headline: The flattest curve in the set — and the best result in the experiment. **The depth control has no chair in it.** At every density the model puts a stool or a box under him and sits him on it.

stand_up.prompt: a man rising to his feet from a seated position
stand_up.headline: The input starts prone on the floor, which is hard for pose recovery — even dense is 140 mm, the highest of the ten. **Read the photoreal row, not the recovered row.** Visually the rise survives to K = 2.

throw.prompt: a man throwing with an overhand motion
throw.headline: **The one clip where the prompt loses.** At every density, dense included, the model hands him a tennis racket and turns the wind-up into a serve. The prompt named no ball, so the model picked its own object.

turn.prompt: a man turning around to face the other direction
turn.headline: Degrades gently and never breaks. Turning around is large and unambiguous — two frames at the ends are enough to specify it.

squat.prompt: a man performing a deep squat
squat.headline: The cleanest monotone slope of the ten, so the best single row for reading the sweep. At K = 2 the model does something interesting rather than wrong: the input holds one squat for six seconds, and given only the two ends it does **repetitions**.

wave.headline: Essentially flat — K = 8 is marginally *closer* to the input than dense. A small motion is fully specified by its endpoints. Foot skate goes 22.6 → **1.3 mm/s**.

slides.title: dense is the worst-looking condition of the five
slides.headline: In **all ten clips** the dense output dresses the person in white or off-white, or bare skin — the model is reproducing the near-white value of the depth silhouette itself. Skin, fabric and lighting come back at K = 8 and keep improving as the control gets sparser.
slides.note: This is the "a video model behaves like a renderer when you specify every frame" point, showing up in appearance rather than in motion.

closing.title: What the sweep shows
closing.headline: For **eight of the ten clips the action survives all the way down to two conditioned frames.** What sparsity costs is not *what* the person does but *when and where* — the input's trajectory, its timing, its specific stride.

columns.title: Where copying breaks
items: **K = 8** — the fast, high-frequency clips: jump, kick, throw
**K = 5** — the locomotion clips: walk, run, stand up
**never sharply** — the slow or near-static ones: sit down, turn, squat, wave. They just drift.

columns.title: The model supplies physics the control lacks
items: **sit down** — no chair in the control, no chair in the prompt. It puts a stool under him at every density and keeps him on it.
**squat at K = 2** — one six-second hold becomes repetitions, which is what a person in a gym actually does.
**Foot contact beats the motion capture** on every slow clip: wave 22.6 → 1.3 mm/s, squat 39.8 → 10.4, sit down 40.8 → 13.7.

columns.title: Where it goes wrong
items: **run** — 5–10× the input's foot skate at every sparse density. It knows what running looks like, not where this runner's feet were.
**throw** — nine times the input's jerk at K = 3, and a tennis racket at every density because the prompt named no ball.
**stand up** — pose recovery struggles with a body prone on the floor. Third experiment to hit this; the fix is a second camera.

closing.punchline: Two frames plus a sentence is enough to produce the **right action**, six seconds long, in a real place. It is not enough to reproduce a **particular performance**.
